title: Orders I Can't Follow
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 21 of 40
content:
The first real fight Danse and I had began with a requisition order.

Not the romantic kind of fight. There was no kissing afterward. No dramatic storm. No convenient enemy to remind us we were on the same side.

It was worse because we both thought we were right.

The Brotherhood wanted a settlement to surrender a pre-War targeting computer found in a collapsed National Guard depot. The settlers wanted to keep it because they had rebuilt the casing into a water-purification controller.

Teagan called it strategic recovery.

The settlement called it not dying of thirst.

Danse read the order twice.

“We can replace their controller.”

“With what?” I asked.

“We’ll find something.”

“When?”

He looked up.

“That isn’t specified.”

“Then we’re taking the thing keeping their water clean on the promise that maybe someone eventually cares enough to come back.”

“It belongs in Brotherhood custody.”

“It belongs to the people using it.”

“The technology is more valuable than one settlement’s improvised application.”

I stared at him.

“You hear yourself?”

His jaw tightened.

“Yes.”

The settlers watched us from across the workshop. Nobody reached for a weapon, but hands were close.

I lowered my voice.

“I’m not doing it.”

Danse’s expression went still.

“That’s a direct order.”

“From Teagan. Not from you.”

“I’m the ranking officer here.”

“Then give me a different one.”

For several seconds the room felt more dangerous than any firefight.

Danse looked from me to the purifier.

“You swore to follow the chain of command.”

“I swore to help protect people.”

“The Brotherhood protects humanity by securing dangerous technology.”

“This is filtering shit out of water.”

One settler coughed into his hand to hide a laugh.

Danse looked furious.

Not because of the language.

Because I had forced the contradiction into the open.

He walked outside.

I followed.

The argument continued behind the workshop where the settlers could not hear.

“You cannot decide which orders matter based on whether you agree with them.”

“Why not?”

“Because that destroys discipline.”

“Good discipline can survive a question.”

“An army where everyone debates every instruction is not an army.”

“I’m not debating where to stand in a firefight.”

“That distinction disappears quickly.”

“Does it?”

“Yes.”

He was breathing hard now.

I had seen Danse angry at mutants, raiders, himself.

This was different.

I was not an enemy.

That made me harder to categorize.

“You think obedience is what makes you good,” I said.

His face closed.

“You don’t get to tell me what I think.”

“You’re right.”

That surprised him.

I continued, “So tell me.”

Danse looked toward the settlement.

“Orders mean someone has considered a problem beyond what’s directly in front of us. Logistics. Long-term risk. Mission priorities. You don’t discard that because one situation feels unfair.”

“That’s the best argument you’ve made.”

He blinked.

“I’m still not taking their purifier.”

His mouth tightened.

“You’re infuriating.”

“So I’ve heard.”

We stood in silence.

Then Danse turned back toward the workshop.

“Wait here.”

He went inside alone.

Twenty minutes later he returned without the targeting computer.

“What happened?”

“I documented the device as operationally integrated into civilian life-support infrastructure and therefore unsuitable for immediate removal without replacement.”

I stared.

“You wrote paperwork at it.”

“I filed an accurate field assessment.”

“You wrote paperwork at it until the order went away.”

“Temporarily.”

I smiled.

Danse pointed one finger at me.

“Do not mistake this for agreement.”

“I wouldn’t dream of it.”

“I still think you handled the situation incorrectly.”

“And yet the settlement has water.”

“That is not the only consideration.”

“No. But it is one.”

His anger faded into exhausted resignation.

“You owe me for the report I’m going to have to file.”

“What do you want?”

He looked at me.

The question hung differently now.

We both remembered the last time he asked what I wanted.

Color touched his face.

“A beer,” he said.

“Coward.”

“Two beers.”

I laughed.

We did not kiss that night.

We sat on the Prydwen observation deck with two beers and argued about authority until midnight.

At some point Danse said, “You know I respect you, even when I think you’re wrong.”

I turned toward him.

“That might be the nicest thing you’ve ever said to me.”

“Don’t make it dramatic.”

“Too late.”

He looked out at the city.

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

I rested my hand on the bench between us.

After a moment, he covered it with his.

Disagreement remained.

So did we.

The report did not make the order disappear so much as bury it under enough procedural language to slow it down.

By the time Teagan sent a reply, Danse and I were halfway back to the airport.

He read the message on his wrist unit while walking.

“Well?” I asked.

“Proctor Teagan is displeased.”

“How tragic.”

“He says field personnel are not authorized to redefine strategic salvage.”

“Tell him field personnel are also not authorized to dehydrate civilians.”

Danse gave me a look.

“I am not writing that.”

“You thought it.”

“I did not.”

“You absolutely did.”

He shut off the display.

“He’s requesting a replacement component before recovery proceeds.”

“So the settlement keeps water until there’s an actual replacement.”

“Yes.”

I smiled.

“Paperwork wins again.”

“This is not a victory.”

“No?”

“No. It is a compromise.”

“Those are allowed to feel good.”

Danse did not answer.

We reached the remains of a diner near the river and stopped beneath its awning when rain began. The place had been picked clean years ago, but the booths still stood beneath cracked windows. We sat opposite each other like two people on the worst date in history.

Danse put his elbows on the table.

“You frightened me back there.”

I had expected another argument.

That was not it.

“What?”

“You challenged an order in front of armed civilians while I was responsible for both the mission and your safety.”

“I wasn’t going to shoot anyone.”

“I know.”

“Then—”

“I did not know what *they* would do.”

His voice stayed calm, which was how I knew the feeling beneath it was not.

“If one of them had panicked and fired, I would have had seconds to decide whether to defend Brotherhood personnel, defend you, or prevent the settlement from turning into a firefight.”

I sat back.

That part I had not considered.

Danse saw it register.

“This is what I mean when I talk about command. An order can be wrong and the way you resist it can still put people at risk.”

The rain tapped against the broken glass.

“You’re right,” I said.

His expression changed.

“Say that again.”

“Don’t make me regret personal growth.”

“I want it documented.”

I kicked his boot lightly under the table.

Then I looked down at my hands.

“I was angry. I saw the purifier and stopped thinking about how close everyone was to their guns.”

“Yes.”

“You saw that before I did.”

“Yes.”

The lack of gloating made the admission easier.

“I’m sorry.”

Danse’s shoulders eased.

“Thank you.”

“But I still think the order was wrong.”

“So do I.”

I looked up sharply.

He frowned.

“I said I disagreed with your handling, not your conclusion.”

“You spent twenty minutes defending the order.”

“I spent twenty minutes defending why orders matter.”

“That is an infuriating distinction.”

“It is nevertheless a distinction.”

I studied him across the old table.

“So you think Teagan was wrong?”

“I think removing functioning life-support equipment without a replacement would undermine the Brotherhood’s stated objective of protecting civilians and damage local cooperation.”

“That was an aggressively Danse way to say yes.”

“Then stop forcing me to explain obvious things.”

I laughed.

He reached across the table and took my hand.

“I need you to understand something else.”

“All right.”

“If the Brotherhood gives me an order I believe is lawful and necessary, I may follow it even when you disagree.”

There was no threat in his voice.

Only honesty.

I squeezed his fingers.

“And I may refuse to help.”

“Yes.”

“You might be angry.”

“Yes.”

“I might be angry too.”

“Almost certainly.”

I smiled.

“Still want to do this?”

Danse looked down at our hands.

“Yes.”

The answer was quiet and immediate.

Something settled between us then. Not agreement. Something better.

The understanding that love was not going to make either of us obedient.

Rain ticked against the leaves around us.

For several minutes neither of us tried to make the disagreement smaller than it was. That mattered. Danse did not promise he would suddenly distrust every Brotherhood order. I did not pretend I could tolerate anything as long as he loved me.

“We may find a line we can’t cross together,” I said.

His face tightened.

“Yes.”

“I hate that answer.”

“So do I.”

“But it’s honest.”

“Yes.”

He looked at our joined hands, then back at me. The fear there was quiet and adult: not fear of an argument, but of discovering love could not solve every difference.

I squeezed his fingers.

For now, honesty was enough.

Danse lifted my hand and, after a brief glance toward the empty road, pressed his mouth to my knuckles.

I stared at him.

He went rigid.

“What?”

“That was smooth.”

His expression became suspicious.

“Was it?”

“Disturbingly.”

“Good.”

“You practiced.”

“I did not.”

“You absolutely practiced.”

Danse stood and started walking back into the rain.

I followed, laughing.

The argument was not over.

Neither were we.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
